name: feature_ablation_and_trend
description: Feature ablation (surface-only vs reference-only vs full) and H1/H2 trend analysis on MVP data. Already executed; registry results from plan-001-fix are taken as given. In worst tier, these in-distribution results are not wrong but are misleadingly optimistic — the 0.06 full-vs-surface gap and the clean H1/H2 split both depend on same-family (Pythia) reference and single-generator setting.
analysis:
In-distribution results are solid. The dual dynamics split appears clean: 3 H2 features drift, 4 H1 features are stationary. Perplexity signal is very strong. However, the worst-tier interpretation is that this clean separation is partly an artifact of the Pythia-Pythia configuration. Subsequent experiments (plan_003, plan_013) will show the H2 drift is partially confounded by length artifacts and reference-model specificity.


These results are from actual execution and look encouraging. But they are entirely in-distribution: single generator (Pythia-2.8B), same-family reference (Pythia-410M), no length control. The 0.82 full F1 benefits from generator-specific artifacts that the reference model can detect precisely because it shares the Pythia architecture. The H2 entropy_mean drift (ρ=-0.68) is strong here because Pythia-410M and Pythia-2.8B share tokenizer and distributional priors — the reference model's perplexity is calibrated to the generator's output distribution. The perplexity monotonic decrease (13.5→1.7) is real but partially reflects the reference model's familiarity with same-family outputs. In worst tier, subsequent experiments reveal these as inflated baselines.

name: cross_generator_evaluation
description: Leave-one-generator-out evaluation across 5 generators. Tests cross-generator generalization. In worst tier, LOGO F1 is poor, especially when holding out non-Pythia generators.
analysis:
Cross-generator generalization fails the 0.58 threshold. The within-family vs cross-family gap (0.625 vs 0.45) reveals the classifier relies on generator-specific artifacts. Gen-0 detection remains passable (~0.75 average) because human-written text is universally distinct, but gen-1 vs gen-2+ discrimination (the core depth signal) collapses cross-family. This undermines Claim 1's generalization requirement. In the reframed paper, this becomes evidence for: "depth estimation requires generator-aware features or larger, more diverse training sets — the task is harder than binary detection because depth artifacts are generator-specific."


The classifier overfits to generator-specific artifacts rather than learning universal depth signatures. Within the Pythia family, generalization is passable (0.61–0.64) because Pythia-2.8B and Pythia-1B share tokenizer, training data (The Pile), and architectural patterns — the Pythia-410M reference model's NLL features are structurally similar for both. But cross-family holdouts (OLMo, Qwen) drop sharply to 0.43–0.48 because: (a) different tokenizers mean surface features (TTR, hapax) have different baseline distributions, (b) the Pythia-410M reference model assigns systematically different perplexity distributions to non-Pythia outputs, creating a domain shift in entropy features, (c) each generator family has its own repetition/diversity profile at each depth, so depth-correlated patterns learned from one family don't transfer. The leave-one-family-out result (0.41 when Pythia held out) confirms the classifier critically depends on Pythia-specific patterns. Overall LOGO F1 of 0.52 is below the 0.58 threshold, killing the cross-generator generalization claim.

name: cross_family_reference_model
description: Test non-Pythia reference models (OLMo-2-1B, Qwen3-0.6B) for feature extraction. Critical falsification test for the dual dynamics framework.

tables.name: Table 5: Entropy_mean Depth Correlation by Reference Model
Table 6: Full Feature Set Classification by Reference Model
Table 7: H1/H2 Stability Across Reference Models

analysis:
The key falsification test triggers: entropy_mean's H2 drift was substantially a Pythia-specific artifact. The dual dynamics narrative ("level features drift, shape features don't, and this cross-cuts surface/reference") collapses because the cross-cutting evidence depended on entropy_mean being a reference feature that drifts. Without it, H2 features are just surface features (TTR, hapax), and H1 features are just reference features — exactly the naive expectation the paper claimed to overturn. The shape feature H1 stability is real but less interesting: it says "distributional shape under any reference model is stable across depth," which is a weaker claim. In the reframed paper, this becomes: "reference-model perplexity as depth proxy is reference-model-dependent — a same-family reference provides much stronger signal, pointing toward an alignment-based explanation of depth discriminability."


Entropy_mean drift (ρ=-0.68 with Pythia reference) largely disappears with non-Pythia references (ρ≈-0.22 OLMo, ρ≈-0.15 Qwen). This happens because entropy_mean is driven by how well the reference model predicts the generated text — when the reference model shares architecture and training data with the generator (Pythia-Pythia), it has calibrated predictions that systematically shift with depth. A cross-family reference model assigns noisier, less calibrated perplexities, washing out the drift signal. The |ρ|<0.3 threshold is breached for both non-Pythia references. Shape features (entropy_std, entropy_max, tail_decay) remain H1-stationary across all references — this is genuinely robust because distributional shape is less sensitive to absolute calibration. But the H2 side of the "dual dynamics" now has only surface features (TTR, hapax_ratio) showing reliable drift (ρ≈-0.28 to -0.30), and these are precisely the features confounded by text length (plan_013). The "dual dynamics cross-cuts surface/reference boundary" claim collapses: the cross-cutting was an artifact of Pythia-Pythia alignment. Classification F1 with non-Pythia reference drops to 0.58–0.63 because the strongest H2 reference feature is now noise.

name: downstream_utility
description: Fine-tune OLMo-1B on depth-stratified data. Compare depth-aware filtering vs binary baselines with 3+ seeds and bootstrap CIs. In worst tier, the advantage is not statistically significant.
analysis:
Downstream utility claim fails significance after proper experimental controls. The improvement exists directionally (1.8% vs 1.2%) but CIs overlap. This was the most anticipated outcome from dream reviews: single-run results are fragile. In reframed paper, report honestly as "directional evidence for depth-quality correlation, insufficient for statistical significance at this sample size" and pivot to the correlation itself (ρ=0.28) as motivation for future work. The perplexity-by-depth monotonic relationship (Table 9) is real and publishable as a descriptive finding — it just doesn't translate into significant downstream filtering advantage.


With proper experimental controls (multiple seeds, CIs, sample-count matching, non-Pythia model), the downstream advantage of depth-aware filtering shrinks to statistical insignificance. Several factors contribute: (1) OLMo-1B is more robust to training data contamination than Pythia-410M (the original MVP model), reducing the overall signal magnitude; (2) with 5 seeds, the variance across runs is substantial (CV≈0.08), swamping the small depth-vs-binary difference; (3) the sample-count-matched comparison shows the original advantage was partly a data size confound — depth-aware filtering keeps more data (it retains gen-1) than binary filtering (which discards all synthetic), so the improvement was partially from having more training data, not from depth stratification per se; (4) bootstrap CIs for the depth-vs-binary comparison overlap substantially (p=0.31), failing significance. The Spearman ρ=0.28 between predicted depth and quality degradation is real but weak, falling in the [0.15, 0.4] worst-tier range. In isolation, this correlation is interesting but not actionable. Claim 3 (downstream utility) cannot be supported as "significantly outperforms binary baselines."

name: prompt_type_comparison
description: Compare continuation vs elaboration vs inspired_rewriting chains. In worst tier, depth signal varies dramatically by prompt type, undermining generalizability.

tables.name: Table 10: Depth Classification by Prompt Type

analysis:
Prompt type is a major moderator of depth signal, challenging ecological validity. In the reframed paper, this becomes a positive finding for the task formulation angle: "Generation depth estimation difficulty depends critically on the semantic coupling between generation steps. Continuation chains (high coupling) preserve depth signal; rewriting chains (low coupling) do not. This connects to attractor cycle theory — semantic-preserving chains converge, while semantically divergent chains don't accumulate distributional drift."


Depth signal is strongly prompt-type dependent. Continuation chains preserve the strongest signal (F1=0.78) because each generation builds directly on the previous output, creating cumulative distributional drift. Elaboration chains weaken the signal (F1=0.55) because the model is asked to expand on a topic rather than continue text — this introduces more creative variation that partially resets the distributional state at each depth. Inspired rewriting shows near-chance depth discrimination (F1=0.47) because the semantic departure from the source is maximal — each depth step is essentially an independent generation conditioned on a theme, not a recursive chain. The entropy_mean drift follows the same pattern (ρ: -0.65/-0.38/-0.18). When training on one prompt type and testing on another, F1 drops to 0.42, showing the features are prompt-type-specific. This means the "depth signal" is partly a "continuation-chain-specific" artifact — real web contamination involves diverse generation patterns, not just continuation.

name: paraphrastic_comparison
description: Compare paraphrasing vs continuation chains. In worst tier, paraphrasing chains converge quickly (as attractor theory predicts), but continuation chains also show limited depth discrimination beyond gen-2.

tables.name: Table 12: Paraphrastic vs Non-Paraphrastic Depth Discrimination

analysis:
Confirms attractor theory prediction for paraphrastic chains. Continuation chains have more signal but also saturate. In reframed paper: "Our empirical results are consistent with attractor convergence — extending the theory to non-paraphrastic chains shows the convergence is slower but still present, bounding practical depth estimation to ~3 useful classes."


Paraphrasing chains converge by depth 2 as attractor theory predicts — gen-2, gen-3, gen-4 are nearly indistinguishable (F1=0.34 for gen-2 vs gen-3). Continuation chains preserve more signal but also saturate by depth 3 — the distributional drift accumulates but with diminishing marginal signal at each step. The worst-tier interpretation: even non-paraphrastic chains have bounded depth discriminability, just with a slightly higher ceiling than paraphrastic ones. The difference (0.78 vs 0.52) confirms continuation chains are better for depth estimation but doesn't rescue the broader generalizability problem — the signal is still chain-type-specific and bounded.

name: cross_model_chains
description: Cross-model chains (different generator per depth step). In worst tier, cross-model chains destroy depth signal because generator identity dominates depth identity.
analysis:
Cross-model chains destroy depth signal — generator identity is a much stronger signal than depth in the feature space. This is the ecological validity nail: real web contamination involves diverse generators. In reframed paper, this honestly motivates future work on generator-invariant depth features and positions the current features as a baseline that works in controlled (single-generator) settings but not in the wild.


Cross-model chains are dramatically harder (F1=0.39, essentially near chance for gen-1 and gen-2+). The reason is fundamental: when generator identity changes at each depth step, the distributional features capture generator identity more than depth. A gen-1 text from Qwen looks more different from gen-1 text from Pythia than gen-1 looks from gen-2 within the same generator. The features (NLL statistics under a fixed reference model) are sensitive to the generator's output distribution, creating a confound where generator variation swamps depth variation. Gen-0 remains detectable (F1=0.65) because human-written text is still distinct from any machine-generated text, but ordinal depth discrimination collapses. This is perhaps the strongest negative result: in the realistic scenario of diverse web generators, depth estimation with these features is not viable.

name: multi_domain_seeds
description: Expand to 4 domains. In worst tier, significant domain variance with some domains showing near-chance performance.
analysis:
Domain is a significant moderator. Factual domains have more signal; creative domains have less. In reframed paper: "Depth estimation difficulty depends on the entropy of the source domain — low-entropy domains (wiki, news) produce more predictable generations with clearer depth drift; high-entropy domains (creative) mask depth signal with natural variation."


Domain variance is substantial. Wikipedia and news seeds (factual, structured prose) show passable performance because LLMs generate predictable continuations with consistent distributional drift. Scientific abstracts show weaker signal because the specialized vocabulary and formulaic structure reduce the distinguishability of human vs machine text at each depth. Creative writing shows near-chance performance because it has the highest natural language variance — the within-class variation in features (e.g., TTR, hapax_ratio) for creative text at any depth is large enough to swamp the between-class (depth) variation. Cross-domain transfer is poor (0.49) because the feature baselines differ across domains. This adds another moderator (domain + prompt type + generator family) that limits the generalizability of depth estimation.

name: finer_grained_ordinal
description: 5-class ordinal classification (gen-0 through gen-4). In worst tier, performance is near chance for finer classes.
analysis:
Five-class is essentially unsolvable with current features. Confirms the 3-class ceiling. In reframed paper, this is a benchmark result: "We establish that 3-class depth estimation (gen-0/gen-1/gen-2+) is the practical ceiling for distributional features, consistent with attractor convergence theory extended to non-paraphrastic generation."


Five-class F1 of 0.28 is barely above chance (0.20 for 5 classes). Gen-0 remains detectable (F1=0.85) and gen-1 is marginally separable (F1=0.42), but gen-2/3/4 collapse into an indistinguishable cluster (F1: 0.18/0.12/0.11). This is because distributional drift between adjacent deep generations is minimal — the marginal change from gen-2→gen-3 in any feature is smaller than the within-class variance. The ordinal MAE of 1.4 means predictions are off by ~1.4 depth levels on average. 72% of misclassifications are between adjacent classes, suggesting some ordinal structure remains but is too weak for practical 5-class discrimination. This validates the attractor convergence prediction: beyond ~3 classes, depth signal is negligible even for non-paraphrastic chains.

name: human_edit_robustness
description: Robustness to simulated human edits. In worst tier, even mild edits substantially degrade performance.
analysis:
Depth features are fragile to post-generation modification. In reframed paper: "Depth estimation is most applicable to unedited generation chains (e.g., automated content farms) and degrades rapidly with human post-processing. This constrains the practical applicability to detection of fully automated pipelines."


Even 5% random word replacement drops F1 by 0.10, and LLM-simulated light editing drops F1 by 0.25. The features are brittle to post-generation modification because both surface features (TTR, hapax) and reference features (entropy statistics) are sensitive to token-level changes. A few word substitutions can significantly alter hapax ratio, TTR, and the reference model's NLL distribution. LLM-simulated editing is worse than random replacement because it systematically "cleans up" the distributional artifacts that depth estimation relies on — an LLM editing gen-3 text makes it look more like gen-1 by smoothing out the accumulated drift. This is a fundamental limitation: any real-world post-processing pipeline (human editing, automated cleanup, grammar correction) will degrade depth signal.

name: ld_score_feature
description: Add LD-Score as feature. In worst tier, LD-Score shows inconsistent behavior — neither clearly H2 nor clearly adding value.
analysis:
LD-Score pre-registered prediction is weakly supported but insufficient to validate the level/shape framework given that the framework is independently undermined by plan_003. In reframed paper: "LD-Score shows weak depth sensitivity, consistent with character-level features capturing some vocabulary drift, but insufficient to serve as independent validation of the dual dynamics hypothesis."


LD-Score shows weak depth correlation (ρ=-0.25), not clearly meeting H2 criteria (slope significant but R²<0.15). Character-level distribution is a noisy proxy for depth — it captures some vocabulary shift but is contaminated by topic and style variation. Adding LD-Score to the feature set provides negligible improvement (+0.005 F1), well within noise. The pre-registered prediction that LD-Score would be a "level feature" exhibiting H2 drift is partially supported (negative ρ) but weak. In worst tier, this fails to provide out-of-sample validation for the level/shape framework because the framework itself is collapsing (plan_003 shows H2 is reference-model-dependent).

name: end_to_end_classifier
description: QLoRA fine-tuned Qwen3.5-0.8B for end-to-end depth classification. In worst tier, end-to-end slightly outperforms handcrafted features, undermining the feature analysis.
analysis:
End-to-end slightly beats handcrafted but shares the generalization failure. In reframed paper: "Both handcrafted and learned features achieve similar in-distribution performance and similar cross-generator degradation, suggesting the depth estimation difficulty is fundamental to the feature space, not a limitation of our specific feature engineering."


End-to-end classification achieves F1=0.83, slightly above the handcrafted 0.78, suggesting that learned representations capture additional signal beyond the 7 distributional features. However, the improvement is modest and the end-to-end model also fails to generalize cross-generator (F1=0.55), indicating the additional signal is also generator-specific. This undercuts the feature analysis contribution: if a fine-tuned LM can slightly beat the handcrafted features, the dual dynamics decomposition is more of an interpretability lens than a competitive method. In worst tier, this result slightly undermines the feature-level analysis without providing a clearly superior alternative — neither approach generalizes.

name: text_length_control
description: Text length confound analysis. In worst tier, length-controlled F1 drops >0.08, revealing that surface features substantially tracked length.

tables.name: Table 20: Feature Depth Correlation Before/After Length Control

analysis:
Length confound is substantial. ~60-68% of surface feature depth correlation was length artifact. Reference features are less affected (19% for entropy_mean) but still impacted. After controlling for length, the full-vs-surface gap nearly vanishes (0.02), meaning reference features' advantage was partially from being less length-confounded, not from capturing genuinely different depth signal. In reframed paper: "We identify text length as a major confound in depth estimation: standard surface diversity metrics (TTR, hapax ratio) primarily track length variation rather than genuine distributional drift. Length-controlled analysis reveals a weaker but real residual depth signal, predominantly carried by reference-model perplexity statistics."


Text length correlates with depth (r=0.42) — deeper generations tend to be shorter as models produce more repetitive/compressed outputs. This correlation confounds both surface features and indirectly reference features. TTR and hapax_ratio are mechanically length-dependent (shorter texts have higher TTR, lower hapax ratio), so their depth correlation (ρ≈-0.3) was partially a length proxy. After length normalization (fixed-window computation), TTR depth correlation drops from -0.31 to -0.12 and hapax from -0.28 to -0.09 — most of the "H2 drift" in surface features was length artifact. Length-controlled full F1 drops by 0.10 (from 0.78 to 0.68), breaching the >0.08 threshold. Notably, reference features also drop (from 0.72 to 0.66) because entropy statistics are affected by text length through the number of tokens evaluated. After length matching (subsampling to equalize length distributions), F1 is 0.70 — real depth signal exists but is substantially weaker than originally measured. The full-vs-surface gap shrinks (0.68 vs 0.63 = 0.05 gap → 0.02 gap after removing length confound from surface features).

name: large_scale_generator
description: Add 7B+ generator (Qwen3-8B-Base). In worst tier, depth signal is minimal at this scale — larger models produce more fluent text that masks distributional drift.

tables.name: Table 21: Depth Classification by Generator Scale
Table 22: Perplexity Dynamic Range by Generator Scale

analysis:
Scale-dependent depth signal degradation is the strongest negative finding and the most publishable result in the worst tier. The log-linear F1-vs-scale relationship is novel empirical evidence connecting depth estimation to model collapse theory: "larger models collapse slower (Gerstgrasser et al.), and correspondingly, depth signal degrades with scale." Note Pythia-2.8B is anomalously high due to same-family reference advantage — once corrected (using cross-family reference, plan_003), it would likely fall closer to the trend line. The perplexity dynamic range analysis (Table 22) provides a mechanistic explanation: reference-model perplexity has less room to drift when the generator is already fluent. In reframed paper, this becomes the central analytical contribution: "Generation depth estimation exhibits a scale-dependent regime: distributional features that reliably detect depth for ≤3B generators fail at 7B+ scale, providing empirical evidence for scale-dependent convergence rates in recursive generation."

The 7B+ generator produces text that is much harder to depth-classify (F1=0.43, near chance for gen-1 and gen-2+). Several mechanisms explain this: (1) larger models have lower perplexity under any reference model, so the absolute perplexity at gen-0 is already closer to machine-generated (8.2 vs 13.5 for human text under Pythia-2.8B reference), reducing the dynamic range for drift detection (4.1 vs 11.8 points of perplexity range across depths); (2) larger models maintain more vocabulary diversity across recursive generations — TTR and hapax ratio drift less because the model's larger capacity preserves lexical variety; (3) the distributional shape of 7B+ outputs is more "human-like" at every depth, compressing the feature space. The F1-vs-generator-size correlation of -0.85 shows a clear scaling law: depth discriminability degrades roughly log-linearly with generator parameters. This connects directly to model collapse literature — larger models collapse slower, producing less distributional drift per recursive step. Gen-0 detection (human vs 7B-generated) is also harder (F1=0.62 vs ~0.90 for smaller generators) because 7B outputs are more human-like on all features.
